# Car Overheats Only on Highway: Diagnosing Flow and Heat Load Issues

When a 1996 Cadillac Sedan DeVille runs perfectly in stop-and-go city traffic but immediately spikes temperature at highway speeds, you are dealing with a classic thermal management failure mode. The engine is not failing; the cooling system architecture is being overwhelmed by a specific load condition that static or low-speed driving does not replicate. You have already replaced the radiator and thermostat, which rules out the most common mechanical failures like a clogged core or a seized valve preventing coolant circulation. However, the symptom of the temperature gauge climbing rapidly while idling at stoplights on the highway suggests the issue lies in how heat is rejected from the engine block to the atmosphere under high airflow conditions.

The primary suspect here is often the cooling fan clutch or the electric fan control module. At low speeds and idle, the engine generates significant heat, but the system relies heavily on the fan to pull air through the radiator when vehicle velocity provides insufficient ram pressure. When you hit 60 mph, the car's forward motion creates a natural draft that pulls air through the radiator fins, effectively cooling the engine. This "ram air" effect is so strong at highway speeds that even a partially inefficient system might hold its own until the vehicle slows down or idles at a traffic light. If you have an electric fan with a thermostat switch (common in this era), the logic is inverted: the fan turns off when airflow is sufficient and turns on when idle. If that electrical circuit fails, opens, or if the relay sticks open, the radiator becomes a dead zone once you stop moving fast enough to maintain natural convection.

Another critical factor is coolant flow dynamics under high load. While a new thermostat ensures the valve opens, it does not guarantee unrestricted flow through the entire loop. A collapsed lower hose or a partially obstructed water pump impeller can handle low-volume circulation fine but choke the system when the engine demands maximum heat transfer at highway RPMs. The water pump in many GM V8 engines of this era uses an external drive and a specific impeller design that can degrade over time. If the impeller has chips or cavitation damage, it moves coolant adequately at idle flow rates but fails to maintain the high GPM (gallons per minute) required when the engine is under heavy thermal stress on the open road.

You must also inspect the radiator cap and pressure integrity. A failed spring in the cap allows the system to boil off at a lower temperature, which might be manageable in town but catastrophic under sustained highway load where heat flux is highest. Additionally, check for air pockets trapped near the thermostat housing or the water pump gasket. These traps can act as insulators that work fine until coolant velocity increases enough to dislodge them, only to cause localized boiling and overheating once flow dynamics change again.

If you are attempting a software-based diagnostic approach similar to how one might debug a system state issue, think of the cooling loop as a feedback control system. The engine ECU monitors coolant temperature and may command fans or adjust fuel mixture (retarding timing) to prevent damage. In some vehicles of this generation, if the engine overheats while idling at highway speeds, the ECU will enter a "limp mode" that cuts ignition or reduces power once it hits a certain threshold to protect the catalytic converter and head gasket. This explains why the car might feel like it is running good in town but feels sluggish or shuts down unexpectedly on the freewayâthe engine is actively protecting itself from thermal failure.

Before replacing expensive components, verify the fan clutch's viscous coupling integrity. If the fan spins freely with your hand when the engine is hot, the internal oil has broken down, and air is no longer being forced through the radiator core when vehicle speed drops below a critical threshold. This specific mechanical failure aligns perfectly with the symptom of overheating only when transitioning from highway speed to idle.
